info.text:
Due Fri Aug 28 at class time. SHM — energy and dynamics (Knight 15.3–15.4).

Sim: Energy-in-SHM sim — mass on a spring with live KE/PE energy bars.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Energy-in-SHM sim in a new tab.

Open the Energy-in-SHM sim. Note the height of the total energy bar, then double the amplitude and read it again.

The total energy is now…

generalfeedback.text:
Four times as large.

The energy stored in the spring at maximum displacement is E = ½kA2. Because the amplitude is squared, doubling A multiplies the energy by 22 = 4. The sim shows the total bar jumping to four times its previous height, not two.

This is the single most useful fact about SHM energy: amplitude is cheap to change and expensive in energy.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — try the sim again.

feedback.text: Correct — and you can see the bar quadruple in the sim.
You scaled the energy in step with the amplitude. Look again at how A enters the energy expression — is it to the first power?
Compare the total bar before and after in the sim — it clearly moves. Something about stretching the spring further must cost energy.
You took a square root where the relationship squares. Write down the energy stored at maximum displacement and check which way the exponent points.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Energy-in-SHM sim in a new tab.

Let the sim run and watch the kinetic energy bar for exactly one full period.

How many times does the KE bar reach its maximum in one period?

generalfeedback.text:
Twice.

The mass passes through the equilibrium position twice per cycle — once moving right, once moving left — and the speed is largest at both of those moments. Kinetic energy depends on v2, so it does not care about direction: both passes give the same maximum.

The consequence: the energy bars cycle at twice the frequency of the displacement.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — try the sim again.

feedback.text: Correct — once on each pass through equilibrium.
Count how many times the mass crosses the middle of its travel in one round trip, not just how many times it goes one way.
You may be counting every turning point as well. Turning points are where KE is at its minimum — watch which bar peaks there.
Change the amplitude in the sim and count again. The size of the peak changes; the number of peaks does not.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Energy-in-SHM sim in a new tab.

Run the sim and pause it at each position below. Match each position of the mass to what the energy bars read there. E is the total energy and A is the amplitude.

generalfeedback.text:
Potential energy grows as the square of displacement: PE = ½kx2, while E = ½kA2. So PE/E = (x/A)2, and KE takes whatever is left.

  • x = A: all potential, no motion.
  • x = 0: all kinetic, spring relaxed.
  • x = A/2: PE is (½)2 = ¼ of E, so KE is ¾E. Note it is not a half-and-half split — that is the trap.
  • x = 0.71A ≈ A/√2: PE is ½E, so the bars are equal.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. For the ones that are not: remember PE depends on x squared, so halfway out is not half the energy. Set the mass at that position in the sim and read the bars.

incorrectfeedback.text: Go back to the sim and pause at each position rather than reasoning it out. Pay particular attention to x = A/2 — the split there is not what most people guess.

name.text: Prep1-D · Readings from the energy sim

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Energy-in-SHM sim in a new tab.

Match each quantity you can determine from the Energy-in-SHM sim to its value or expression. A is the amplitude, k the spring constant and T the period.

generalfeedback.text:
Total energy at amplitude A: ½kA2 — all of the energy is elastic at the turning point.

Time between successive KE maxima: T/2 — the mass crosses equilibrium twice per period, so the energy bars run at double frequency.

Number of times the speed is zero per cycle: 2 — the two turning points.

Displacement where KE = PE: A/√2 — setting ½kx2 = ½(½kA2) gives x = A/√2 ≈ 0.71A, not A/2.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. Two of these you can read directly off the sim by timing the bars; the other two come from where the energy sits at the turning point. Check the row you are least sure of against the sim.

incorrectfeedback.text: Work through them in the sim one at a time — time the gap between KE peaks, count the stops per cycle, and find the position where the two bars match.

subquestion.text: Number of times the speed is zero per cycle

info.text:
Due Mon Aug 31 at class time. Vertical oscillations and the simple pendulum (Knight 15.5–15.6).

Sim: Pendulum sim — adjustable length and gravity, with a period read-out.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Pendulum sim in a new tab.

In the Pendulum sim, set L = 1.0 m and note the period. Now set L = 4.0 m and read it again.

The period…

generalfeedback.text:
Doubles.

T = 2π√(L/g), so the period grows with the square root of the length. Quadrupling L multiplies T by √4 = 2 — a 1.0 m pendulum has T ≈ 2.0 s and a 4.0 m pendulum has T ≈ 4.0 s.

Square-root dependence is why pendulum clocks need such long rods for such modest gains in period.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — read the two periods off the sim again.

feedback.text: Correct — √4 = 2.
You scaled the period in step with the length. Check whether L sits under a square root in the period expression, then compare your prediction with the sim's read-out.
You have the direction backwards — the sim shows a long pendulum swinging more slowly, not faster. Watch it before answering.
The read-out clearly changes when you move the length slider. Length is one of the two things the period does depend on.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Pendulum sim in a new tab.

Keep the length fixed and change g from 9.8 m/s2 to 1.6 m/s2 (lunar gravity). Read the new period.

The period becomes roughly…

generalfeedback.text:
About 2.5 times longer.

T = 2π√(L/g), so T scales as 1/√g. The ratio is √(9.8/1.6) = √6.1 ≈ 2.5.

Weaker gravity means a weaker restoring torque, so each swing takes longer — the same reason astronauts move in slow motion.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — compare the two read-outs in the sim.

feedback.text: You used the full ratio of the two g values. The period depends on g under a square root — take the root of that ratio and compare with the sim.
Right factor, wrong direction. Weaker gravity gives a weaker restoring pull — does that speed the swing up or slow it down? The sim will settle it.
You may be thinking of the bob's mass, which really does cancel. Gravity does not — move the g slider and watch the read-out.

name.text: Prep2-C · Limits of the small-angle result

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Pendulum sim in a new tab.

With the length fixed, release the pendulum from 5°, then from 45°, and compare the two measured periods carefully.

The period at 45° is…

generalfeedback.text:
Slightly longer at 45°.

T = 2π√(L/g) comes from the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ. At larger angles sin θ is smaller than θ, so the real restoring torque is weaker than the ideal one and the swing takes a little longer — roughly 4% longer at 45°.

This is the honest version of “the period is independent of amplitude”: it is a limit, not a law, and the sim lets you see where it starts to fail.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — look at more decimal places in the sim's read-out.

feedback.text: Correct — about 4% longer, which is exactly where the small-angle approximation starts to show.
That is what the textbook formula predicts — but the formula assumed a small angle. Look at the sim's read-out to more decimal places and see whether it really holds at 45°.
Right that it changes, wrong direction. Compare sin θ with θ itself at 45° — which is bigger, and so is the true restoring torque stronger or weaker than the ideal one?
Far too large — the sim shows a change of a few percent, not a factor of two. The small-angle result is a good approximation even here, just not a perfect one.

name.text: Prep2-D · One change at a time

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Pendulum sim in a new tab.

Make each change in the Pendulum sim one at a time, leaving everything else alone, and match it to its effect on the period T.

generalfeedback.text:
T = 2π√(L/g). Only two things appear in it, and both under a square root.

  • Length × 4 → T × 2 (√4 = 2).
  • g × 4 → T × ½ (g is in the denominator).
  • Bob mass × 4 → T unchanged. Mass never appears — gravity's pull and the inertia it must move grow together and cancel exactly.
  • 5° → 10° → T essentially unchanged. Both angles are well inside the small-angle regime; the change is far under 1%.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. Change one slider at a time in the sim and write down the period before and after — the two “times four” rows do not give the same factor, and one of the four changes nothing at all.

incorrectfeedback.text: Go back to the sim and test each change separately. Two of these move the period, and two of them do not.

info.text:
Due Wed Sep 2 at class time. Traveling waves, standing waves and superposition (Knight 16.1–16.3).

Sim: Wave explorer — equation-driven single traveling wave (A, λ, k, φ, f, with a Traveling-wave toggle).

name.text: Prep3-A · Wave speed from the sim

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

In the Wave explorer, set λ = 4 m and f = 2 Hz.

What wave speed does v = fλ give?

generalfeedback.text:
8 m/s.

v = fλ = (2 Hz)(4 m) = 8 m/s.

What the relation means physically: in one period the pattern advances exactly one wavelength. Two periods per second, four metres per period, so eight metres per second.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — check your two sim settings.

feedback.text: Correct.
You divided instead of multiplying. In one period the wave moves forward by one whole wavelength — that should tell you which operation you want.
You divided the wrong way round. Check the units: metres per second has to come out of metres times per-second.
An extra factor of 2 has crept in — possibly from a period-versus-frequency mix-up. Re-read the two numbers you set in the sim.

name.text: Prep3-B · What moves in a traveling wave

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

Turn on the Traveling wave toggle in the Wave explorer and press Play. First follow a single crest as it moves across the screen. Then shift your attention to one fixed location: pick a vertical gridline and watch only the height of the curve where it crosses that line.

As the wave passes, the string at that fixed location…

generalfeedback.text:
It moves up and down about its rest position, repeating every period T.

A traveling wave carries a disturbance — and the energy in it — from one place to another, but the medium itself stays put. Each point of the string performs simple harmonic motion about its own rest position, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, with the same period T as the wave. What sweeps across the screen is the shape y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt), not the material.

This is the core of the wave model, and the thing most often gotten backwards: the pattern travels, the medium does not.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — watch one fixed gridline, not one crest.

answer.text: moves up and down about its rest position, repeating every period T

feedback.text: Correct — the pattern travels; the material at each point just oscillates in place.

answer.text: travels to the right, keeping pace with the crests

feedback.text: That is what the pattern does. Fix your eye on one gridline instead of following a crest — does the material at that line actually go anywhere, or does it only rise and fall in place?

answer.text: shifts to the right until the wave has gone by, then stops

feedback.text: Let the sim keep running. Fresh crests arrive at your chosen gridline again and again — does the disturbance there ever settle, and does that point drift sideways at all?

answer.text: stays flat; only the crests and troughs elsewhere are moving

feedback.text: Watch the curve's height right at your chosen gridline as first a crest and then a trough reach it. If the whole waveform is passing through that spot, its height there cannot stay fixed.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

The sim draws y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt). Match each symbol to the expression the sim's read-outs confirm for it.

generalfeedback.text:
k = 2π/λ — the wave number counts radians of phase per metre.

ω = 2πf — the angular frequency counts radians of phase per second.

v = fλ — equivalently ω/k, the speed at which a given phase travels.

T = 1/f — seconds per cycle rather than cycles per second.

Two of these are about space, two about time, and v is the bridge between them. Step any one control in the sim and the linked read-outs move together.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. Sort them first: which symbols describe the wave in space and which in time? Then step the matching control in the sim and watch which read-outs follow.

incorrectfeedback.text: Use the sim's linked read-outs: step λ and see what changes with it, then step f and do the same. The pairings follow directly.

name.text: Prep3-D · One control at a time

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

Change one control at a time in the Wave explorer and match it to what you see happen on screen.

generalfeedback.text:
Increase A: crests get taller, nothing else. Amplitude is purely vertical — it leaves λ, k and the cycle count alone.

Increase λ: each wave is longer, so fewer full waves fit across the screen.

Increase f at fixed λ: v = fλ grows, so the pattern travels faster.

Increase φ: a positive phase makes the wave reach each value sooner, sliding the whole curve to the left.

The first one is the standard trap — amplitude is easy to confuse with “how wavy” the picture looks.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. This one really has to be done in the sim — step each control on its own and watch exactly one thing change. Amplitude is the one most people get wrong.

incorrectfeedback.text: Open the sim and step one control at a time, resetting between changes. Each of these four produces a visibly different effect.

answer.text: Fewer full waves fit on screen
More full waves fit on screen

info.text:
Due Fri Sep 4 at class time. Waves on strings and musical instruments (Knight 17.1–17.2).

Sim: Standing Waves — Strings & Pipes. In String mode the wave speed comes from tension and linear density, v = √(T/μ); in Pipe mode it is the speed of sound and the boundary is set by how many ends are open.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Standing Waves sim in a new tab.

In the Standing Waves sim, keep Medium on String and Ends on Fixed–Fixed, and select the fundamental (n = 1) on a string of length L.

Its wavelength is…

generalfeedback.text:
2L.

Both ends are fixed, so both must be nodes, and adjacent nodes sit half a wavelength apart. The fundamental has nothing but those two end nodes and a single antinode in the middle — so the string holds exactly half a wavelength, and λ = 2L.

The general rule follows: λn = 2L/n.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — look at how much of a full wave shape the string actually holds.

feedback.text: Correct — the string holds half a wavelength.
A very common answer. Look closely at the fundamental in the sim: is that a whole wave shape between the ends, or half of one?
You have the relation inverted. Recall that adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, then read off the distance between the two fixed ends.
That is the Fixed–Free case — a quarter-wave. Here both ends are held down, so both are nodes. Try switching Ends to Fixed–Free in the sim to see where 4L comes from.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Standing Waves sim in a new tab.

With Medium on String and Ends on Fixed–Fixed, step the sim to the third harmonic (n = 3).

How many nodes appear between the two fixed ends?

generalfeedback.text:
Two.

The nth harmonic has n antinodes and n − 1 interior nodes, plus the two fixed ends. For n = 3 that is three bellies separated by two stationary points.

Counting nodes on screen is the fastest way to identify which mode you are looking at — no formula needed.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — count the stationary points on screen again.

feedback.text: Correct — three bellies, two interior nodes.
You matched the node count to the harmonic number. Count the bellies (antinodes) instead — there are three of those, and the nodes sit between them.
That is the second harmonic. Check which mode the sim is actually showing, then count again.
Only the fundamental has no interior nodes. Look for points on the string that never move as the animation runs.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Standing Waves sim in a new tab.

In String mode, swap to a heavier string — a larger linear density μ — at the same Tension and Length.

The fundamental frequency…

generalfeedback.text:
Goes down.

The wave speed is v = √(T/μ), so more mass per metre means a slower wave. The wavelength of the fundamental is fixed at 2L by the string's length, so f1 = v/2L must fall.

This is why the low strings on a guitar or piano are the thick ones: same length, same rough tension, more mass per metre, lower pitch.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — try the density control in the sim.

feedback.text: Correct — the same reason bass strings are thick.
Check where μ sits in the wave-speed expression — numerator or denominator? Then think of a real instrument: are its thick strings the high notes or the low ones?
The read-out moves when you change the density. The wavelength is pinned by the string's length, so any change in wave speed has to show up as a change in frequency.
Wrong direction, and the size is not right either — the dependence is a square root, so the factor is milder than that.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Standing Waves sim in a new tab.

In String mode with Fixed–Fixed ends, step through the modes and match each harmonic to its wavelength on a string of length L.

generalfeedback.text:
λn = 2L/n: the nth harmonic fits exactly n half-wavelengths between the fixed ends.

  • n = 1: half a wave on the string, λ = 2L.
  • n = 2: one full wave, λ = L.
  • n = 3: one and a half waves, λ = 2L/3.
  • n = 4: two full waves, λ = L/2.

The wavelengths get shorter as 1/n, so the frequencies climb as n — the harmonic series.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. For each mode, count how many half-wavelengths fit between the fixed ends in the sim — that number is the harmonic.

incorrectfeedback.text: Step through the modes in the sim and count half-wavelengths on the string for each one. The pattern λ = 2L/n should become visible.

name.text: Prep4-E · A flute and a clarinet

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Standing Waves sim in a new tab.

Switch Medium to Pipe (sound). Set Ends to 2 open (a flute) and note the fundamental frequency. Now set Ends to 1 open — one end closed, like a clarinet — keeping the length the same.

Compared with the open–open pipe, the closed pipe's fundamental frequency is…

generalfeedback.text:
Half as large (about an octave lower).

A pipe open at both ends has a displacement antinode at each end, so it holds half a wavelength: λ1 = 2L and f1 = v/2L. Closing one end forces a node there while the open end stays an antinode, so the pipe now holds only a quarter wavelength: λ1 = 4L and f1 = v/4L — half the open pipe's value.

That octave drop is why a clarinet plays lower than a flute of similar length. The closed pipe also drops all the even harmonics (only n = 1, 3, 5… survive), which is a big part of why a clarinet sounds "hollower" than a flute.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — compare the two fundamental read-outs in the sim, and look at how much of a wave fits in the tube each way.

feedback.text: Correct — a closed pipe holds a quarter-wave instead of a half-wave, so λ doubles and f halves.
Wrong direction. Closing an end makes the standing wave longer (a quarter-wave now spans the tube), and a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.
The two fundamental read-outs differ. The boundary condition at the closed end changes which standing waves fit, so the fundamental wavelength — and pitch — changes too.
Right direction, wrong factor. Compare the fundamental wavelengths: 2L for open–open versus 4L for open–closed — a factor of two, not four.

info.text:
Due Mon Sep 7 at class time. Interference (Knight 17.3–17.5).

Sim: Two-source interference — two in-phase sources with a movable detector and a path-difference read-out.

name.text: Prep5-A · Path difference of one wavelength

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Two-source interference sim in a new tab.

In the Two-source interference sim, move the detector until the path difference reads exactly one wavelength.

What do you get there?

generalfeedback.text:
Fully constructive — a maximum.

A path difference of one whole wavelength puts the second wave exactly one full cycle behind the first, which is the same as being perfectly in step. The crests arrive together and the amplitudes add.

The general condition: Δr = mλ for m = 0, 1, 2, … gives constructive interference.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — check the detector read-out in the sim.

feedback.text: Correct — a whole wavelength of delay is no delay at all.
You may be thinking “any path difference means they are out of step.” Ask instead how much of a cycle one wavelength of extra travel corresponds to.
Interference at a full-wavelength offset is not partial — the sim shows one of the two extremes. Which one?
Both sources are still emitting; the detector still reads something. Move it to that position in the sim and look.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Two-source interference sim in a new tab.

Now move the detector until the path difference reads 1.5λ.

The result is…

generalfeedback.text:
Complete cancellation.

Only the fractional part of the path difference matters. The whole wavelength puts the waves back in step, and the remaining half-wavelength puts them exactly opposite — crest against trough.

The general condition: Δr = (m + ½)λ gives destructive interference. So 0.5λ, 1.5λ and 2.5λ all cancel alike.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — check the detector read-out in the sim.

feedback.text: Correct — the half-wavelength is what matters.
You may have rounded 1.5λ to the nearest whole wavelength. Strip off the whole wavelength — what fraction of a cycle is left over?
The 1.5 is a path difference in wavelengths, not a multiplier on the amplitude. Read the detector in the sim instead.
Try both positions in the sim and compare the read-outs. Does adding one whole wavelength of extra travel change the phase relationship at all?

name.text: Prep5-C · Source separation and fringe spacing

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Two-source interference sim in a new tab.

Increase the separation d between the two sources and watch the whole interference pattern.

The maxima…

generalfeedback.text:
Move closer together.

With the sources further apart, a smaller change in angle is enough to add another whole wavelength to the path difference, so successive maxima crowd in. Quantitatively the fringe spacing goes as λ/d.

Widely separated sources therefore give a finely detailed pattern — the trade-off that makes diffraction gratings useful later in the course.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — drag the separation control and watch the pattern.

feedback.text: Correct — spacing goes as λ/d.
The intuitive guess, and the sim disagrees. Drag the separation slider slowly and count how many maxima appear across the pattern before and after.
The pattern visibly rearranges in the sim. Source separation is one of the two things that set the fringe spacing.
The maxima are still there, just differently spaced. Look closely — there may simply be more of them than before.

name.text: Prep5-D · Path difference to detector reading

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Two-source interference sim in a new tab.

Set each path difference in turn in the sim and match it to what the detector reads there. The two sources are in phase.

generalfeedback.text:
Whole wavelengths of path difference leave the waves in step; half-wavelengths turn them exactly opposite.

  • Δr = 0 → maximum (in step by definition).
  • Δr = λ/2 → zero (crest on trough).
  • Δr = λ → maximum (a full cycle of delay is no delay).
  • Δr = 3λ/2 → zero (one whole wavelength plus a half).

So the whole rule is: integer multiples of λ are bright, half-integer multiples are dark.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. Only the fractional part of the path difference matters — strip off any whole wavelengths first, then decide.

incorrectfeedback.text: Set each value in the sim and read the detector. Look for the pattern in which ones are bright and which are dark before you commit.
